warmup.q: A switch has these cases, in this order: case Card c when c.corporate() -> 290;, then case Card c when c.network() == AMEX -> 350;, then case Card c -> 30;. What fee does a corporate AMEX card get?
options: 350, because the more specific rule wins
290, because cases are tried from the top and the first match wins
It doesn't compile: two guarded cases for the same type are ambiguous
It doesn't compile: the AMEX case is dominated by the corporate case
warmup.why: Java tries the cases in order and runs the first one whose pattern matches and whose guard is true. Both guards are true for a corporate AMEX card, so the corporate rule wins. javac doesn't compare guards, so it can't tell that the AMEX rule is shadowed for corporate cards: a guarded case never dominates another. Put the AMEX rule first.

sections.h: A pattern switch is checked, an instanceof chain is not
sections.html:
A pattern is a test with a binding. Card c asks "is this value a Card?" and, if it is, gives you a new variable c of type Card. Pattern matching came to Java in steps. JDK 16 made instanceof patterns final (JEP 394): the type test and the cast become one, and the binding is in scope wherever the test is known to have passed.

Java
if (!(o instanceof Card c)) return "not a card";
return "last four: " + c.last4();          // c is in scope: the test can't have failed here
Kotlin
if (o !is Method.Card) return "not a card"
return "last four: ${o.last4}"             // smart cast: o is a Card from here on

JDK 21 made pattern switch final (JEP 441), together with record patterns (JEP 440). It's tempting to read a pattern switch as a tidier if/else if chain. It is more than that, and the differences are the reason to prefer it:

  • javac checks that it is exhaustive. An instanceof chain that forgets Wallet compiles without a word and falls into its final else. The switch that forgets it fails with the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. A pattern switch used as a statement must be exhaustive too, and the message then says switch statement.
  • javac checks dominance: a case that can never match is a compile error (section 3).
  • It has defined null rules (section 4).
  • It compiles to one invokedynamic call to SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch, which picks the case, plus a synthetic arm that throws MatchException if no case matches at run time.

Kotlin has had most of this for years. A when with a subject checks exhaustiveness over a sealed type, whether you use it as an expression or a statement, and smart casts merge the is check and the cast. With the JDK 21 target, kotlinc 2.4 even compiles that when to the same typeSwitch call; its fallback arm throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException instead. What Kotlin doesn't have is the subject of the next section.

try.title: See which one the compiler catches
steps: Run PatternBasics (or PatternBasicsKt) with the command below.
Delete the Wallet line from viaChain and run. Put it back, then delete the Wallet case from viaSwitch and run again. Which mistake did the compiler catch?
From labs/, run javap -c -p modernjava/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/PatternBasics.class and find typeSwitch and MatchException in viaSwitch.
Run the same javap on modernjava/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/PatternBasicsKt.class and look at viaWhen.

code.title: PatternBasics.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; /** The same dispatch three ways: an instanceof chain, a guard clause, and a pattern switch. */ public class PatternBasics { sealed interface Method permits Card, Transfer, Wallet {} record Card(String network, String last4) implements Method {} record Transfer(String iban) implements Method {} record Wallet(String provider) implements Method {} // an if-chain: javac never checks that it covers every Method static String viaChain(Method m) { if (m instanceof Card c) return "card " + c.network() + " ****" + c.last4(); else if (m instanceof Transfer t) return "transfer from " + t.iban(); else if (m instanceof Wallet w) return "wallet " + w.provider(); else throw new IllegalStateException("unreachable?"); } // a pattern switch: javac checks that every Method is covered static String viaSwitch(Method m) { return switch (m) { case Card c -> "card " + c.network() + " ****" + c.last4(); case Transfer t -> "transfer from " + t.iban(); case Wallet w -> "wallet " + w.provider(); }; } // flow scoping: after the negated test returns, c is in scope for the rest of the method static String last4(Object o) { if (!(o instanceof Card c)) return "not a card"; return "last four: " + c.last4(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Method[] all = { new Card("VISA", "1111"), new Transfer("DE89370400440532013000"), new Wallet("Paywave") }; for (Method m : all) { System.out.println(viaChain(m) + " | " + viaSwitch(m)); } System.out.println(last4(all[0]) + ", " + last4("4111")); } }

alt.title: PatternBasics.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo sealed interface Method { data class Card(val network: String, val last4: String) : Method data class Transfer(val iban: String) : Method data class Wallet(val provider: String) : Method } // an if-chain: kotlinc never checks that it covers every Method fun viaChain(m: Method): String = if (m is Method.Card) "card ${m.network} ****${m.last4}" // smart cast: m is a Card here else if (m is Method.Transfer) "transfer from ${m.iban}" else if (m is Method.Wallet) "wallet ${m.provider}" else throw IllegalStateException("unreachable?") // when with a subject: kotlinc checks that every Method is covered fun viaWhen(m: Method): String = when (m) { is Method.Card -> "card ${m.network} ****${m.last4}" is Method.Transfer -> "transfer from ${m.iban}" is Method.Wallet -> "wallet ${m.provider}" } // a smart cast lasts for the rest of the function after a negated check returns fun last4(o: Any): String { if (o !is Method.Card) return "not a card" return "last four: ${o.last4}" } /** The same dispatch three ways: an if-chain, an early return, and a when. */ fun main() { val all = listOf(Method.Card("VISA", "1111"), Method.Transfer("DE89370400440532013000"), Method.Wallet("Paywave")) for (m in all) { println(viaChain(m) + " | " + viaWhen(m)) } println(last4(all[0]) + ", " + last4("4111")) }

try.expect: Both versions print the same three lines and last four: 1111, not a card. Without its Wallet branch the chain still compiles, and the run crashes on the wallet with the chain's IllegalStateException. Without its Wallet case the switch doesn't compile: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (kotlinc: Add the 'is Wallet' branch or an 'else' branch.). In the bytecode, viaSwitch has invokedynamic ... typeSwitch and new java/lang/MatchException; the Kotlin viaWhen has the same typeSwitch call and new kotlin/NoWhenBranchMatchedException.

sections.h: Record patterns take the data apart in the label
sections.html:
A type pattern tests a type and binds one variable. A record pattern also takes the record apart, through its accessors, and each part can be a pattern too. Here are the first fee rules from this lesson's lab, next to the closest Kotlin. The when after each pattern is a guard, an extra condition that section 3 covers.

Java
return switch (charge) {
    case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card(var net, var corp), var r) when net == Network.AMEX -> bps(m, 350);
    case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card(var net, var corp), var r) when corp -> bps(m, 290);
    // ...
};
Kotlin
val m = charge.amount.minor
return when (val method = charge.method) {    // pick the nested part out first
    is Card if method.network == Network.AMEX -> bps(m, 350)
    is Card if method.corporate -> bps(m, 290)
    // ...
}

Read the Java label from the outside in. The selector, the value in switch (...), must be a Charge. Its amount() must match Money(long m, var ccy), which binds m and ccy. Its method() must be a Card, which binds net and corp. And region() binds to r. With var, javac infers each type from the record's components. Patterns are positional and type-checked: put String x where a record has an int and javac stops with incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. Generic records work too. Over sealed interface Result<T>, the case Ok<T>(var v) binds v as a T. Record patterns also work in instanceof, as in if (o instanceof Line(Point(var x, var y), var to) && x == 0).

Kotlin has no record patterns. The closest tools are smart casts on nested properties, as in the twin above, and positional destructuring, val (from, to) = line, through component1() and component2(). Destructuring has a trap Java's patterns mostly avoid: it goes by position, not by name. With data class Payment(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long), the line val (amountMinor, id) = payment compiles without a warning and puts the id into amountMinor. Kotlin 2.3.20 added name-based destructuring as an Experimental feature, behind -Xname-based-destructuring; its name-mismatch mode warns about exactly this line. Java's record patterns are positional as well, but every component is type-checked, so most swaps fail to compile. Two var bindings of the same type can still be swapped silently, so keep the record header in front of you.

try.title: Take a line apart
steps: Predict the third line of output, then run RecordPatterns.
In describe, change Point(int x2, int y2) to Point(String x2, int y2) and run. Read the error, then undo it.
Run the Kotlin twin, RecordPatternsKt, and read its last line.

code.title: RecordPatterns.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; import java.util.List; /** Record patterns: take a record apart in the case label, nested as deep as you like. */ public class RecordPatterns { record Point(int x, int y) {} record Line(Point from, Point to) {} sealed interface Result<T> permits Ok, Err {} record Ok<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {} record Err<T>(String message, Throwable cause) implements Result<T> {} static String describe(Line line) { return switch (line) { case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(int x2, int y2)) when x1 == x2 -> "vertical at x=" + x1 + " len " + Math.abs(y2 - y1); case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when y1 == y2 -> "horizontal at y=" + y1; case Line(Point from, Point to) -> "diagonal " + from + "->" + to; }; } static <T> String show(Result<T> r) { return switch (r) { case Ok<T>(var v) -> "ok " + v; // T inferred for v case Err<T>(var msg, var cause) when cause != null -> "err " + msg + " caused by " + cause.getClass().getSimpleName(); case Err<T>(var msg, var cause) -> "err " + msg; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(1, 0), new Point(1, 5)))); System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(0, 3), new Point(7, 3)))); System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(0, 0), new Point(2, 2)))); System.out.println(show(new Ok<>(List.of(1, 2)))); System.out.println(show(new Err<>("boom", new RuntimeException()))); Object o = new Line(new Point(0, 0), new Point(9, 9)); if (o instanceof Line(Point(var x, var y), var to) && x == 0 && y == 0) { // patterns in instanceof too System.out.println("from origin to " + to); } } }

alt.title: RecordPatterns.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) data class Line(val from: Point, val to: Point) sealed interface Outcome<out T> { data class Ok<T>(val value: T) : Outcome<T> data class Err(val message: String, val cause: Throwable?) : Outcome<Nothing> } data class Payment(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long) // Kotlin can't take records apart in a when branch: match the outer type, then read the properties fun describe(line: Line): String { val (from, to) = line // positional destructuring via component1/2 return when { from.x == to.x -> "vertical at x=${from.x} len ${kotlin.math.abs(to.y - from.y)}" from.y == to.y -> "horizontal at y=${from.y}" else -> "diagonal $from->$to" } } fun <T> show(r: Outcome<T>): String = when (r) { is Outcome.Ok -> "ok ${r.value}" is Outcome.Err if r.cause != null -> "err ${r.message} caused by ${r.cause::class.simpleName}" // guard: Kotlin 2.2+ is Outcome.Err -> "err ${r.message}" } /** The Kotlin side: smart casts and positional destructuring instead of record patterns. */ fun main() { println(describe(Line(Point(1, 0), Point(1, 5)))) println(describe(Line(Point(0, 3), Point(7, 3)))) println(describe(Line(Point(0, 0), Point(2, 2)))) println(show(Outcome.Ok(listOf(1, 2)))) println(show(Outcome.Err("boom", RuntimeException()))) val o: Any = Line(Point(0, 0), Point(9, 9)) if (o is Line && o.from.x == 0 && o.from.y == 0) { // smart cast after the is check println("from origin to ${o.to}") } // destructuring goes by position, not by name: this compiles, with no warning, and swaps the values val (amountMinor, id) = Payment("p1", 500) println("swapped names: amountMinor=$amountMinor id=$id") }

try.expect: vertical at x=1 len 5, horizontal at y=3, diagonal Point[x=0, y=0]->Point[x=2, y=2], then ok [1, 2], err boom caused by RuntimeException and from origin to Point[x=9, y=9]. The String change fails with incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. The Kotlin twin prints the same results with smart casts, and then swapped names: amountMinor=p1 id=500: positional destructuring put the id into amountMinor without a warning.

sections.html:
Cases are tried from the top, and the first one whose pattern matches and whose guard is true wins. The guard is the when clause after the pattern. That makes order part of the meaning. A corporate AMEX card matches both of the first two lines below, so whichever comes first sets its fee:

Java
case CardCharge(var net, var corp, var amt) when net == Network.AMEX -> amt * 350 / 10_000;
case CardCharge(var net, var corp, var amt) when corp -> amt * 290 / 10_000;
case CardCharge(var net, var corp, var amt) -> amt * 30 / 10_000;
Kotlin
is Charge.Card if c.network == Network.AMEX -> c.amountMinor * 350 / 10_000
is Charge.Card if c.corporate -> c.amountMinor * 290 / 10_000
is Charge.Card -> c.amountMinor * 30 / 10_000

Guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, in either language. The compiler can't prove that a set of guards covers every value, so a family of guarded cases must end with an unguarded case of the same pattern. Delete the last line above and javac says the switch doesn't cover all possible input values, while kotlinc asks you to Add the 'is Card' branch. You can predict javac's verdict yourself. List the permitted subtypes of the selector's type. Cross off each one that has an unguarded case, or that sits under a sealed parent with an unguarded case. Inside record patterns, check combinations, not columns: for each subtype of the first component, the cases that start with it must between them cover the second component, and so on. With Pair(Red a, Red b) and Pair(Green a, Light b), the Red cases cover only Red in second place, so Pair(Red, Green) is missing. What is left over is what JDK 27 prints under missing patterns:.

javac also rejects a case that can never be reached: this case label is dominated by a preceding case label. That happens when an earlier unguarded case already matches everything the later one could: case String s after case CharSequence cs, case Integer i when i > 0 after an unguarded case Integer i, a constant case 1 after case Integer i, or any pattern after default. A guarded case never dominates, which is why javac accepts the two guarded card rules in either order. Only your tests notice the difference. kotlinc has no dominance check at all: put the unguarded is Charge.Card first and it compiles without a warning, and every card pays 0.3%. Kotlin guards (is T if condition) have been stable since Kotlin 2.2; one limit is that a guard can't follow several conditions joined by commas.

Several patterns can share one arm only if they bind nothing. On JDK 21 that rule makes such arms awkward: case Capture c, Refund r -> fails with illegal fall-through from a pattern, so you write two arms. JDK 22 made unnamed patterns final, and case Capture _, Refund _ -> is legal. _ also stands in for a component you don't need, as in case Authorize(var code, _). On JDK 21 it is a preview feature, and javac stops with unnamed variables are a preview feature and are disabled by default.

code.title: GuardsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; /** Cases are tried from the top, and the first one that matches wins. Guards decide the order. */ public class GuardsDemo { enum Network { VISA, MASTERCARD, AMEX } sealed interface Charge permits CardCharge, TransferCharge {} record CardCharge(Network network, boolean corporate, long amountMinor) implements Charge {} record TransferCharge(boolean instant, long amountMinor) implements Charge {} static long fee(Charge c) { return switch (c) { case CardCharge(var net, var corp, var amt) when net == Network.AMEX -> amt * 350 / 10_000; // 1 case CardCharge(var net, var corp, var amt) when corp -> amt * 290 / 10_000; // 2 case CardCharge(var net, var corp, var amt) -> amt * 30 / 10_000; // 3 case TransferCharge(var instant, var amt) when instant -> 50; case TransferCharge t -> 20; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { Charge[] charges = { new CardCharge(Network.AMEX, false, 10_000), new CardCharge(Network.AMEX, true, 10_000), new CardCharge(Network.VISA, true, 10_000), new CardCharge(Network.VISA, false, 10_000), new TransferCharge(true, 10_000), }; for (Charge c : charges) { System.out.printf("%-62s fee %d%n", c, fee(c)); } } }

alt.title: GuardsDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo enum class Network { VISA, MASTERCARD, AMEX } sealed interface Charge { data class Card(val network: Network, val corporate: Boolean, val amountMinor: Long) : Charge data class Transfer(val instant: Boolean, val amountMinor: Long) : Charge } // guards in when branches (`is T if condition`) are stable since Kotlin 2.2 fun fee(c: Charge): Long = when (c) { is Charge.Card if c.network == Network.AMEX -> c.amountMinor * 350 / 10_000 // 1 is Charge.Card if c.corporate -> c.amountMinor * 290 / 10_000 // 2 is Charge.Card -> c.amountMinor * 30 / 10_000 // 3 is Charge.Transfer if c.instant -> 50 is Charge.Transfer -> 20 } /** Branches are tried from the top, and the first one that matches wins. Guards decide the order. */ fun main() { val charges = listOf( Charge.Card(Network.AMEX, false, 10_000), Charge.Card(Network.AMEX, true, 10_000), Charge.Card(Network.VISA, true, 10_000), Charge.Card(Network.VISA, false, 10_000), Charge.Transfer(true, 10_000), ) for (c in charges) { println("%-62s fee %d".format(c, fee(c))) } }

try.expect: The corporate AMEX card pays 350. After the swap it pays 290 and nothing else changes: the corporate rule now matches it first. With line 3 on top, javac rejects lines 1 and 2 with this case label is dominated by a preceding case label, while the Kotlin version compiles and charges every card 30. Without line 3, javac reports the switch expression does not cover all possible input values and kotlinc asks for the 'is Card' branch. On JDK 22+ the preview file prints authorize with A1B2C3, fail: insufficient funds and not allowed yet twice; JDK 21 rejects the _.

refs.title: Guard conditions in when expressions (Kotlin docs)

sections.html:
switch has always thrown NullPointerException on a null selector, and a pattern switch keeps that rule unless you opt in with case null:

Java
return switch (currency) {
    case null -> "missing";
    case "EUR" -> "euro";
    default -> "other";          // default alone does not catch null
};
Kotlin
return when (currency) {         // currency is a String?
    null -> "missing"
    "EUR" -> "euro"
    else -> "other"              // without the null branch, null lands here
}

case null, default -> handles both in one arm. For most code, the OpenJDK guide on sealed switches prefers something simpler: reject null before the switch with Objects.requireNonNull, because a null that reaches business logic is a bug somewhere upstream. Kotlin settles the question in the type system. A when over a String? must handle null somewhere (kotlinc says Add the 'null' branch or an 'else' branch. if it doesn't), and nothing throws.

Inside a record pattern, null follows a rule that surprises everyone once. A nested record pattern never matches null, but a nested type pattern that covers the whole component type does. So with case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when x1 == x2 first and case Line(Point from, Point to) second, a Line whose start is null skips the first case and lands in the second, with from bound to null. Change the second case to Line(Point(var a, var b), Point to) and javac still calls the switch exhaustive, but that Line now matches nothing and the switch throws MatchException.

That points at the bigger limit: exhaustive is a compile-time promise. javac checks the switch against the subtypes it can see when it compiles. The values it can't see, which the Amber design notes call the remainder, are handled at run time. Compile a client against Status permits Active, Closed, then recompile only the hierarchy with a third status, Frozen, and run the old client: its switch throws java.lang.MatchException. An enum switch with no default does the same when it meets a constant added later. The old Kotlin when throws kotlin.NoWhenBranchMatchedException. You don't write code for the remainder, but in a deployment that mixes old and new jars, this is the exception you will see. Recompile the client and javac turns it back into a compile error.

try.title: Feed a switch null, then a stranger
steps: Run NullDemo and NullDemoKt and compare their first lines.

In the Java describe, change case Line(Point from, Point to) to case Line(Point(var a, var b), Point to) (and use a and b in the text). Predict: does it compile? What happens to the line with a null start?
Run the separate-compilation experiment in labs/modernjava/javac/remainder. The five commands are at the top of Client.java.

code.title: NullDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; /** What a switch does with null: at the top level, and inside a nested pattern. */ public class NullDemo { record Point(int x, int y) {} record Line(Point from, Point to) {} static String plain(String currency) { return switch (currency) { // the old rule: a null selector throws case "EUR" -> "euro"; default -> "other"; }; } static String withNull(String currency) { return switch (currency) { case null -> "missing"; // opt in to null case "EUR" -> "euro"; default -> "other"; }; } static String nullOrDefault(Object o) { return switch (o) { case String s -> "text " + s; case null, default -> "null or other"; // one arm for both }; } static String describe(Line line) { return switch (line) { case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when x1 == x2 -> "vertical"; case Line(Point from, Point to) -> "other line " + from + " -> " + to; // Point from also matches null }; } public static void main(String[] args) { try { System.out.println(plain(null)); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("plain(null): NullPointerException"); } System.out.println("withNull(null): " + withNull(null)); System.out.println("nullOrDefault: " + nullOrDefault(null) + " / " + nullOrDefault(42)); System.out.println("line, null start: " + describe(new Line(null, new Point(1, 1)))); } }

alt.title: NullDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo data class Spot(val x: Int, val y: Int) data class Segment(val from: Spot?, val to: Spot?) // in Kotlin the type says whether null can arrive, and when compares with equals: null never throws fun plainWhen(currency: String?): String = when (currency) { "EUR" -> "euro" else -> "other" // null lands here } fun withNullWhen(currency: String?): String = when (currency) { null -> "missing" "EUR" -> "euro" else -> "other" } fun nullOrElse(o: Any?): String = when (o) { is String -> "text $o" else -> "null or other" } fun describeSegment(s: Segment): String { val from = s.from val to = s.to return when { from != null && to != null && from.x == to.x -> "vertical" else -> "other line $from -> $to" // you write the null case yourself } } /** What when does with null: the nullable type decides, and nothing throws. */ fun main() { println("plainWhen(null): ${plainWhen(null)}") println("withNullWhen(null): ${withNullWhen(null)}") println("nullOrElse: ${nullOrElse(null)} / ${nullOrElse(42)}") println("line, null start: ${describeSegment(Segment(null, Spot(1, 1)))}") }

try.expect: Java prints plain(null): NullPointerException; Kotlin prints plainWhen(null): other, because its when compares with equals and the type allowed null. Both print missing, then null or other twice, then a line whose start is null. After the change in step 2 the switch still compiles, and the null-start line throws java.lang.MatchException. The experiment prints active, priority 1, then sealed switch: java.lang.MatchException and enum switch: java.lang.MatchException from the old client; recompiling it gives two does not cover all possible input values errors.

analogy: A pattern switch is the routing table in a card network's switch centre. Each row says "if the message looks like this, with these fields, send it there", and messages are checked against the rows from the top. Record patterns let a row look inside the message (BIN range, currency, merchant category) instead of only at its type, and a guard is an extra condition on a row. The network also proves that every possible message has a row, so nothing is dropped. The analogy breaks at the edges: a real routing table can fall back to a default route without anyone noticing a gap, while javac refuses a switch with a gap, and a message type invented after the table was built makes the Java switch throw instead of routing it somewhere.
world: Most code that consumes payment events or issuer responses is a dispatch on shape: "a refund of a card payment over 500 EUR goes to manual review", "a decline with a retryable code goes back on the queue". Written as nested instanceof checks and casts, those rules hide gaps; written as one switch with record patterns, javac finds the missing shapes and the order of the rules is visible in one place. Two production habits follow from this lesson. Validate non-null at the edge (the REST resource, the Kafka deserializer) with Objects.requireNonNull, so switches never see null. And treat a MatchException in the logs after a deploy as "a service was built against an older version of a shared model jar": rebuild it, and the compiler will show you the cases to add.
mistake: The mistake that ships is a guarded rule placed after a broader guarded rule, such as the corporate-card rate above the AMEX rate. Both cases are guarded, so javac accepts either order and reports nothing, and every corporate AMEX card is charged the corporate fee. People make it because they read the switch as a set of rules, when it is an ordered list. Write the most specific rule first, end each family with an unguarded case, and give every rule a test case that matches more than one guard, as the lab's ruleOrder test does.

compare.title: The fee rules in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Fees.java
java.html: static long fee(Charge charge) { return switch (charge) { case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card(var net, var corp), var r) when net == Network.AMEX -> bps(m, 350); case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card(var net, var corp), var r) when corp -> bps(m, 290); case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card c, var r) when r == Region.EEA || r == Region.UK -> bps(m, 30); case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card c, var r) -> bps(m, 150); case Charge(var amount, BankTransfer(var instant), var r) when instant -> 50; case Charge(var amount, BankTransfer t, var r) -> 20; case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Wallet w, var r) when m < 1_000 -> 0; case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Wallet w, var r) -> bps(m, 100); }; }

kotlin.title: Fees.kt
kotlin.html: fun fee(charge: Charge): Long { val m = charge.amount.minor val r = charge.region return when (val method = charge.method) { is Card if method.network == Network.AMEX -> bps(m, 350) is Card if method.corporate -> bps(m, 290) is Card if r == Region.EEA || r == Region.UK -> bps(m, 30) is Card -> bps(m, 150) is BankTransfer if method.instant -> 50 is BankTransfer -> 20 is Wallet if m < 1_000 -> 0 is Wallet -> bps(m, 100) } }

compare.note: The rules, the order and the exhaustiveness check are the same in both: the first matching branch wins, guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, and neither version needs a default. The difference is where the data comes apart. Java's record patterns reach into Charge, Money and Card in the label and bind the parts. Kotlin can only test the type of the value it switches on, so the twin pulls method out first, switches on that, and reads charge.amount.minor by hand. javac also checks dominance, which kotlinc doesn't, and Java's switch has explicit null rules, where Kotlin leaves null to the type system.

worked.title: Rewrite a refund router as one switch

steps.say: This code decides how a refund is paid back. It compiles, it has tests, and it has a bug the compiler can't see. Read it and look for a payment method it forgets.
steps.code: static String refundRoute(Event event) { if (event instanceof Refund r) { if (r.payment().method() instanceof Card c) { if (c.network() == Network.AMEX && r.amountMinor() > 50_000) return "manual review"; return "card refund"; } if (r.payment().method() instanceof BankTransfer) return "bank refund"; } return "ignore"; }

alt.html: fun refundRoute(event: Event): String { if (event is Refund) { val method = event.payment.method if (method is Card) { if (method.network == Network.AMEX && event.amountMinor > 50_000) return "manual review" return "card refund" } if (method is BankTransfer) return "bank refund" } return "ignore" }

steps.say: Name the shapes you care about, most specific first, and let each label take the event apart. Event is sealed (Refund, Capture) and so is Method, so the switch needs no default.
steps.code: static String refundRoute(Event event) { return switch (event) { // 1. the special case first case Refund(Payment(var id, Card(var net, var corp)), long amt) when net == Network.AMEX && amt > 50_000 -> "manual review"; // 2. then the general cases, one per method case Refund(Payment(var id, Card c), long amt) -> "card refund"; case Refund(Payment(var id, BankTransfer t), long amt) -> "bank refund"; // 3. events that need no refund case Capture c -> "ignore"; }; }

alt.html: fun refundRoute(event: Event): String = when (event) { is Refund -> when (val method = event.payment.method) { // 1. the special case first is Card if method.network == Network.AMEX && event.amountMinor > 50_000 -> "manual review" // 2. then the general cases, one per method is Card -> "card refund" is BankTransfer -> "bank refund" } // 3. events that need no refund is Capture -> "ignore" }

steps.say: That doesn't compile, in either language: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (kotlinc: Add the 'is Wallet' branch). A refund of a wallet payment matches no case. The old chain had the same gap and returned "ignore", so wallet refunds were silently never paid. The compiler found the bug the tests missed. Add the case.
steps.code: case Refund(Payment(var id, Wallet w), long amt) -> "wallet refund"; // the case the chain forgot

alt.html: is Wallet -> "wallet refund" // the case the chain forgot

steps.say: On JDK 22 or newer, replace the bindings you never use with _, so a reader sees at a glance which parts each rule depends on. Kotlin's version already names only what it reads.
steps.code: // JDK 22+ case Refund(Payment(_, Card(var net, _)), long amt) when net == Network.AMEX && amt > 50_000 -> "manual review"; case Refund(Payment(_, Card _), _) -> "card refund"; case Refund(Payment(_, BankTransfer _), _) -> "bank refund"; case Refund(Payment(_, Wallet _), _) -> "wallet refund"; case Capture _ -> "ignore";

alt.html: // Kotlin uses _ only for unused lambda parameters and destructured components val (_, amountMinor) = refund // skip the payment, keep the amount

lab.title: A fee calculator over a sealed hierarchy
steps: Run the tests: all eight fail. Read the rule list in the Javadoc of fee. The order of the rules is the order of your cases.
Write fee as one switch over the Charge, with record patterns and guards and no default. Start with the AMEX rule, and run the tests after every two or three cases.
Write label. It needs a case null, and the wallet needs care: what does Wallet(String p) bind when the provider is null?
When all eight pass, swap your AMEX and corporate cases and run the tests again. Which test catches it? Swap them back.
Delete your last, unguarded card case and compile. Read the error, then put it back.
hints: The first case can be case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card(var net, var corp), var r) when net == Network.AMEX -> bps(m, 350);.
Each method family must end with an unguarded case: one for Card, one for BankTransfer, one for Wallet. Otherwise javac says the switch doesn't cover all possible input values.
fee doesn't need case null: a pattern switch without one throws NullPointerException, which is what the test expects.
Wallet(String p) matches a wallet whose provider is null, with p bound to null. Put case Wallet(String p) when p == null before the general wallet case.

drill.title: A guarded switch from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Given sealed interface Settlement permits Settled, Failed, record Settled(long amountMinor) and record Failed(String code, boolean retryable), write nextStep(Settlement s): settlements of 1,000,000 minor units or more return "review", other settlements "done", retryable failures "retry", and other failures "alert". No default. Then write it in Kotlin with when guards.

answer.html: static String nextStep(Settlement s) { return switch (s) { case Settled(long amt) when amt >= 1_000_000 -> "review"; case Settled st -> "done"; // unguarded: closes the Settled family case Failed(var code, var retryable) when retryable -> "retry"; case Failed f -> "alert"; // unguarded: closes the Failed family }; }

alt.html: fun nextStep(s: Settlement): String = when (s) { is Settlement.Settled if s.amountMinor >= 1_000_000 -> "review" is Settlement.Settled -> "done" // unguarded: closes the Settled family is Settlement.Failed if s.retryable -> "retry" is Settlement.Failed -> "alert" // unguarded: closes the Failed family }

recap: A pattern switch is checked for exhaustiveness and dominance and has defined null rules. An instanceof chain gets none of that.
Record patterns take records apart in the case label, nested, through the accessors, with var inference and type checks.
Cases run top to bottom and the first match wins. Guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, so end each guarded family with an unguarded case.
A null selector throws unless you write case null, and default doesn't catch it. A nested type pattern matches a null component; a nested record pattern doesn't.
Exhaustive is a compile-time promise. A subtype or enum constant added later makes an old client throw MatchException (NoWhenBranchMatchedException in Kotlin).
JDK 21's exhaustiveness errors are generic and JDK 27 lists the missing patterns. _ needs JDK 22, and primitive patterns are still a preview feature.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "If the switch over our sealed PaymentEvent compiles with no default, it can never fail at run time, right?" Explain, in your own words, when it can, and what you would do about each case.
explain.answer: Exhaustive is checked at compile time, against the subtypes javac could see then. At run time two things can still slip through. First, null: a null selector throws NullPointerException unless there is a case null, and a null inside a nested record pattern can make the switch throw MatchException. I'd reject nulls at the boundary with Objects.requireNonNull so they never reach the switch. Second, separate compilation: if the event library adds a subtype and our service runs the new jar without being recompiled, the old switch throws MatchException for the new event. The fix is to rebuild against the new version, and then the compiler shows every switch that needs a case. Adding a default to hide it would be worse, because the new event would quietly take the default branch.

deeper.html:
Two newer features build on this lesson. Neither belongs in the labs, which compile for JDK 21.

Primitive types in patterns have been a preview feature in every JDK from 23 to 27, and they are still a preview in the JDK 28 builds. They let a switch over an int use type patterns and guards, and let instanceof ask whether a value fits another primitive type exactly:

Java
// JDK 25: java --enable-preview --source 25 preview/PrimitivePatterns.java
static String riskBand(int score) {
    return switch (score) {
        case 0 -> "no score";
        case int s when s < 300 -> "high risk (" + s + ")";
        case int s -> "low or medium risk (" + s + ")";
    };
}
Kotlin
// Kotlin has always allowed conditions on any subject
fun riskBand(score: Int): String = when {
    score == 0 -> "no score"
    score < 300 -> "high risk ($score)"
    else -> "low or medium risk ($score)"
}

Without the preview flags, JDK 25 stops with primitive patterns are a preview feature and are disabled by default. Treat the syntax as likely to change until it is final.

The second feature is better error messages. JDK 27's javac lists what a non-exhaustive switch is missing, under a missing patterns: line, in the form Rect _ for a type and Pair(Red _,Green _) for a nested record pattern. That one change makes nested exhaustiveness errors much easier to read: on JDK 21 the same Pair switch only says it doesn't cover all possible input values, and you work out the missing combination yourself.

One habit to avoid: don't write case _ when .... JDK 25's javac accepts it, but the JLS doesn't allow it, and a fix in JDK 28 development (JDK-8385488) makes javac reject it. Write default or a real type pattern instead.
